layoutProps.eyebrow: Lesson 1 · Two ways to draw the world

items.title: The chart on the wall
items.markdown: A portolan chart drawn in Majorca around 1375, redrawn so it can be read.
items.alt: A portolan chart of the Mediterranean and the Black Sea on a calfskin: rhumb lines in three colours, harbour names written inland at every angle, a wind rose, a scale of miles. The whole sea is tilted, Italy lying almost flat.

props.caption: The chart on the wall, redrawn: Majorca, about 1375. By the end of the course, you will answer each of the visitor's puzzles.

props.markdown: Around 630, Isidore of Seville summed up the known world in a diagram any student could draw from memory. An **O**, the Ocean, encircles the land. Inside it, a **T** of waters divides the land into three parts: the Mediterranean is the stem, the Don and the Nile are the arms. Asia, the largest part, fills the upper half.
props.aside: Isidore's *Etymologiae*, an encyclopaedia read all through the Middle Ages.

props.figureAlt: A T-O world map: a ring of ocean round a disc divided by a T of waters into Asia above, Europe bottom left and Africa bottom right, with Jerusalem at the crossing and Paradise at the top.

items.title: Asia
items.markdown: The largest part of the world fills the upper half, towards the rising sun.

items.title: Europe
items.markdown: Europe takes the lower left quarter.

items.title: Africa
items.markdown: Africa takes the lower right quarter.

items.title: The T of waters
items.markdown: The Mediterranean is the stem of the T, the Don and the Nile its arms.

items.title: Jerusalem
items.markdown: Jerusalem sits where the waters of the T cross, at the centre of the world.

items.title: Paradise
items.markdown: Paradise sits in the far east, at the top of the map.

props.caption: Isidore's T-O diagram, redrawn. East is at the top: the side of the rising sun, where medieval Christians placed the Garden of Eden.

props.title: Where “orienting” comes from
props.markdown: To orient a map once meant to turn it towards the *orient*, the east. North at the top became the habit only centuries later.

props.stem: A visitor asks why the world map in the first room has the east at the top. What do you answer?

options.text: Medieval compasses pointed east, so every map was drawn that way
options.feedback: A compass needle points north, then as now. World maps were not drawn with a compass at all.

options.text: East is where the sun rises and Paradise lies: the story starts there
options.feedback: Yes: a mappa mundi is read from the east, like a story from its beginning.

options.text: It was drawn for the pilgrims sailing east towards the Holy Land
options.feedback: Pilgrims could not steer by it: it shows the meaning of the world, not its distances.

props.markdown: The great world maps of the thirteenth century fill the T-O with everything a learned Christian knew. On the **Hereford map**, drawn around 1300, **Jerusalem** sits at the centre and Paradise at the top, among cities and rivers, scenes from the Bible and the animals and peoples of distant lands. It is a book in one picture, made to be read and meditated, not a guide to any road.
props.aside: Hereford Cathedral, England. Its Mediterranean is a narrow ribbon: the map shows *what* the world holds, not *where*.

props.alt: Detail of the Hereford map south of the Nile: a river in blue, people with faces on their chests or shoulders, a basilisk, a lion, beasts and their red and black labels, beside a band of dark ocean.
props.markdown: South of the Nile on the Hereford map: people with faces on their chests, a basilisk and other beasts.
props.caption: Detail, from a printed reproduction.

props.alt: A round world map: a ring of ocean, three parts divided by a T of waters, a city at the centre and a golden island at the top.

props.markdown:
**Purpose**: to show the world's history and what it means.

**At the top**: the east, and Paradise.

**Made from**: books: the Bible, Roman geographers, travellers' tales.

**Used**: in churches and libraries, to read and to meditate.

props.alt: A corner of a sea chart: the coast of Spain and the Balearic Islands, harbour names written across the land, and black, green and red lines radiating from two points.

props.markdown:
**Purpose**: to sail from one harbour to the next.

**At the top**: nothing: you turn the chart.

**Made from**: compass bearings and the miles between harbours.

**Used**: on board, at the chart table, with a ruler and dividers.

props.alt: Four panels of the Catalan Atlas on vellum: Europe, the Mediterranean and North Africa criss-crossed by rhumb lines, a wind rose in the Atlantic, the names of the north written upside down, kings and caravans in Africa.
props.caption: A real one: the Catalan Atlas, drawn in Majorca in 1375 (Bibliothèque nationale de France). Its rhumb lines and harbour names share the vellum with kings, caravans and marvels.

props.title: Two jobs, not old and new
props.markdown: The two kinds of map were made in the same centuries, for different readers. Neither is a clumsy draft of the other: the Catalan Atlas above sets a sea chart and a world of kings and marvels side by side.
